1:
Who receives this law is the first thing Ellicott notices, and he takes the change to be deliberate. The rules for detecting the disease were spoken to Moses and Aaron together; the rules for purifying a man cured of it go to Moses alone, who is to pass them on to Aaron and his sons. He suspects the reason lies in Moses' office — designed by God as the great lawgiver and teacher of the priesthood as much as of the laity. Gill reads the opening the same way, the law given to Moses to be delivered to Aaron, whose successors would chiefly execute it.

That there is a law of cleansing at all settles a question about the disease. Henry draws the conclusion out: the plague of leprosy was not incurable. Uzziah's did continue to the day of his death and Gehazi's was entailed upon his seed, but Miriam's lasted seven days, and it may often have worn off in the course of time. Though God contend long, he says, he will not contend for ever.

The whole first stage happens outside the camp, and Keil and Delitzsch explain what that placing means. This act restores a man regarded as dead to the fellowship of the living members of the covenant nation, and so is performed where he has been living, not where the sanctuary stands. Ellicott has him conducted from his seclusion to an appointed place on the border, and identifies that journey with the one Christ commanded of the men he healed (Matthew 8:4). Clarke comes at it from the other end: since the priest alone could pronounce a man clean, and without that pronouncement no readmission to civil or religious society was possible, the healed man had no choice but to present himself.

Henry finds the mercy in the direction of the traffic. When the leper was shut out and could not go to the priests, it was well that the priests might come to him — and without contracting the defilement another visitor would have contracted. The men ordered to attend the sick were the men whose lips should keep knowledge; those under affliction need teaching in how to bear it and how to profit by it, so that the word goes with the rod. Applied to the spiritual disease, the pattern cuts both ways: those we withdraw from are not to be counted enemies but admonished as brethren (2 Thessalonians 3:15), and those whom grace has brought to repentance are to be received back with tenderness, as Paul directed at Corinth (2 Corinthians 2:7-8). Ministers hold the declarative power of loosing as well as binding, and must use both so that sinners are not encouraged by an excess of lenity nor penitents discouraged by an excess of severity.

Calvin builds his whole comment on the limit set to the priest's office. He is commanded to cleanse, and forbidden to cleanse anyone not already clean — by which God keeps the honour of the cure to himself while establishing a discipline in his church. It belongs to God only to forgive sins, so the minister can absolve no one God has not absolved first; absolution is not in the power or will of man, and his part is to proclaim a sentence already passed (Isaiah 43:25). Yet Calvin will not let that make the ministry idle. Since faith purifies the heart by receiving the testimony God offers through a human mouth, the man who testifies that we are reconciled is justly reckoned to take away our pollution — and the discipline stands with it, that whoever has been cast out by public authority is not received again except on professing repentance and a new life. Wesley states the same distinction in a line: God alone healed the man really, the priest only declaratively.
4:
Four things are fetched, and the second-Temple lawyers had settled specifications for each. The birds had to be sparrows, on the reasoning that leprosy punished calumny and these birds are proverbial for their constant twitter — which is why the Vulgate and the Authorised margin say sparrow. The cedar had to be a foot and a half long; the scarlet a band of wool weighing a shekel; the hyssop a handbreadth, and not the Greek or Roman varieties but the common sort grown in gardens. Clarke is less confident about the birds — any clean bird might have served.

What the four made was a tool. Clarke describes the assembly: the cedar stick for a handle, the hyssop and the living bird bound to it with the crimson wool, the bird fixed tail-downward to be dipped; Ellicott has the priest tie hyssop and cedar lengthwise, then spread the bird's wings and tail around them and dip all four together. Gill notes that the fetching was not the priest's own work — he commanded, and the leper or his friends supplied what was named.

Why these four is answered symbolically, and the answers largely agree. Cedar does not readily rot, so Henry and Wesley take it for soundness restored to flesh that had been putrefying; the scarlet for colour returning to a skin the disease had made white as snow; the hyssop, being fragrant, for the removal of the smell that went with the sickness. Ellicott records an older reading that runs the opposite way — that the cedar, belonging to the loftiest of trees, stands for the haughtiness which called the affliction down, and the hyssop for the humility without which it cannot be cured. The highest and the lowest together give the leper purity.

The killing is deliberately not a sacrifice, and the details follow. Gill and Wesley both note that the priest did not do it himself and that it happened outside the camp, away from the altar. Clarke describes the vessel: spring water — living water, chosen because water from pits and wells is often putrid, and in a rite of purifying everything must be as pure as possible — poured into a clean earthen dish, the bird killed over it so the blood ran in. Ellicott's account is stricter, the vessel new and the measure a quarter of a log; afterwards a hole was dug and the bird buried before priest and patient.

The mixture of blood and water is where Henry and Wesley both stop. Water and blood came from the pierced side (John 19:34), and Christ comes into a soul not by water only but by water and blood (1 John 5:6). Some, Henry says, make the slain bird Christ dying for our sins and the living bird Christ rising for our justification, the dipping of the one in the blood of the other showing that the merit of the death is what makes the resurrection effectual; Wesley states that reading without qualification, while Clarke warns that running analogies between type and thing typified is precarious — the general design is plain, the particulars are not.

Where the sprinkling landed is disputed. Gill reports three opinions — the veil over the face, the back of the hand, the forehead — while Ellicott has both hand and forehead. On the number there is no dispute: seven times, for a complete cleansing, which is why Naaman washed seven times in Jordan (2 Kings 5:10), and why the psalm asks to be purged with hyssop (Psalms 51:7). Then the bird goes. Wesley has it returning to its former abode, and Ellicott makes the release a picture of the man's own liberty, restored and unrestrained. Henry watches it climb instead, and reads the upward flight as a charge not to spend the restored life on earthly things.
8:
Being pronounced clean is not the end of it, and Henry marks the gap. The priest declares the disease gone; the man must then make himself as clean as he can from every remnant of it, and is given time to do so. Those who have the comfort of remission, he adds, are to cleanse themselves with the same care from all filthiness of flesh and spirit, since everyone who has that hope in him will be concerned to purify himself.

The razor goes over everything. Keil and Delitzsch specify head, beard, eyebrows and in fact the whole body; Ellicott says the same and notes that the Levites were consecrated by a comparable shaving (Numbers 8:7). Two reasons are offered for so thorough a stripping. Clarke's is practical — that the water might reach every part of the surface, no place being left where defilement could remain; he mentions that the Egyptian priests shaved the whole body every third day on the same principle. Wesley's is diagnostic: with the hair gone the man's soundness could be seen, and nothing was left in which the disease might lurk and return.

What the washing is for divides the witnesses. Ellicott denies outright that it disinfects anything, since on his reading the disease was not contagious; the clothes are washed as an act of purification, of the kind performed after every sort of defilement. Wesley takes the opposite view of the same provisions, and his reason for keeping the man out of his own tent is that some leprosy still lurking in him might break out and infect his household. Gill sits between them, washing the clothes so that no remains of the infection should be left in them and no ill scent carried to others.

On what the week outside the tent actually meant, Ellicott passes on a reading of some delicacy. The man is back in the camp but not in his own house, and the authorities of the second Temple took the phrase as a euphemism for abstinence — the Chaldee paraphrase renders it that he shall sit outside the tent of his habitation and not come near the side of his wife for seven days — so that no fresh impurity should interrupt the period of preparation.

The seventh day repeats the whole business, and the repetition is the hinge of the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch divide the ritual there: the first act had restored a man reckoned dead to the living members of the nation, and the second, beginning with this second shaving and bathing, restores him to fellowship with God and admission to the sanctuary. Ellicott makes the same division and points out that the first stage gave back social and civil privileges only. He would render the last clause as bathing rather than washing the flesh, the word meaning simply self or body, and objects that the Authorised Version translates one deliberate ritual phrase in three different ways where it should be identical throughout. He adds one detail from the later Temple that shows the rite still had a place of its own: restored lepers bathed in a chamber at the north-western corner of the Court of the Women, called the chamber of the lepers.
10:
Calvin makes the eighth day carry the weight of the whole section. Infants were grafted into the church on the eighth day after the uncleanness they brought from the womb; here the eighth day restores men who are, in the cure received, as it were born again — those whom leprosy had banished being accounted dead. The sacrifice appointed is a renewal of a circumcision that had been in some measure effaced. Having said that much he stops: the meaning of all these things is not clear to him, and he would not have his readers too curious about them.

The offerings sort themselves by function. Clarke assigns each in a line — the sin offering for the man's impurity, the trespass offering for his transgression, the flour for a gratitude offering acknowledging his cleansing — with the second he-lamb kept for the burnt offering that closes the rite. Ellicott's interest is in what is unusual about the list. A meat offering does not ordinarily accompany a trespass or a sin offering, and where one lamb is brought a single omer is the rule; three are required here, which the second-Temple authorities explain as standing in for the drink offering the expiatory sacrifices would otherwise have carried. The measure of oil is stranger still, the word occurring four times in this section and nowhere else in the Hebrew scriptures — six hen's eggs, on the reckoning current in the first century, which is Wesley's figure too; he takes the oil itself for a sign of God's grace and of the man's healing.

Where he stands to present them is the point Ellicott presses hardest. Expiation has not yet been made, so the man may not enter the court of Israel; the priest came out to the gate of Nicanor between that court and the Court of the Women, and there he stood facing the sanctuary — which is what being before the LORD amounts to in his case. Even the laying on of hands had to be managed through the opening: Gill and Ellicott both describe him putting both hands through the gate onto the victim, which was killed at once. And killed by somebody else — on ordinary occasions the offerer did his own slaughtering on the north side of the altar, but here appointed men did it, and Ellicott would render the clause in the passive to match the Chaldee, which supplies a slaughterer outright.

Henry reads the same standing-at-the-door as an invitation rather than a barrier. The mercies of God oblige us to present ourselves to him (Romans 12:1), and when he restores the liberty of his ordinances after sickness we should take the first opportunity to use it — as Christ found the healed man in the temple soon after (John 5:14), and as Hezekiah, asking for a sign that he should go up to the house of the Lord, was asking for a sign that he should recover. What we present must be presented by the priest who made us clean. Wesley keeps the division sharp underneath all this: the healing is ascribed to God, while the cleansing is the priest's act performed by the rites God prescribed.

The trespass offering carries the peculiarities. Ellicott notes that both the lamb and the log of oil were waved before the Lord — done with no other trespass or sin offering, and the only occasion on which an entire victim was waved. Wesley finds the doctrine in the choice of offering: a trespass offering teaches that sin caused the leprosy, and every disease, and points past the body to the diseases for which men must fly to God in Christ. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree on what became of the flesh — most holy, the officiating priest's perquisite, eaten by him and the males of his household within the court.
14:
Blood goes on three points of the body, and Ellicott reconstructs the choreography from second-Temple practice. Two priests caught the blood of the trespass offering, one in a vessel and one in the hollow of his hand; the first threw his against the wall of the altar, the second carried his to the man waiting in the porch of Nicanor. Because the blood of an expiatory sacrifice could not be taken beyond the court of Israel, the priest stayed inside the gate and the man put his head through it to have the cartilage of his right ear touched, then his right hand for the thumb, then his right foot for the toe — though he might put all three through at once to save time. Gill gives the same account of the two priests and the two portions of blood.

Why these three and why the right side is answered the same way by everyone who asks. Ellicott takes the right members as the strongest and so the ablest to execute the will of God, dedicated henceforward to his service, and notes that the identical rite consecrated the priests. Henry seizes on that: the very ceremony used at the consecration of Aaron and his sons is used here, a mortification to them, since the same purification was necessary for a priest as for a leper. Wesley reads the three points as a restoration of ordinary use — the man is free now to hear God's word in the appointed places, to touch person or thing without defiling it, and to go where he pleases. Ellicott adds the hard corollary of so physical a rite: a man without a right thumb, toe or ear could never be cleansed at all.

Then the oil, and the same three points again. Ellicott would render the clause about the left palm strictly — the officiating priest poured the oil into the palm of a second priest, though he might use his own — and observes that the Authorised Version dropped the word priest and supplied his own to settle a question the Hebrew leaves open. The sprinkling was done inside the court, the priest facing the Holy of Holies and dipping his finger afresh for each of the seven sprinklings on the floor — which Keil and Delitzsch explain as consecrating the oil to God before any of it touched the man.

What is left goes onto the blood. Ellicott has both priests return to the gate, the oil laid on the ear and thumb and toe already marked, so that it stands literally upon the blood of the trespass offering; the remnant is put — not poured, there being too little in a hollow hand — on his head. The bulk of the log stayed behind as the priests' perquisite, eaten within the sacred precincts like the flesh.

The order — blood first, oil after — is where Henry finds the doctrine, quoting Bishop Patrick: the blood a token of forgiveness, the oil of healing, since God first forgives our iniquities and then heals our diseases (Psalms 103:3). Wherever the blood of Christ is applied for justification the oil of the Spirit is applied for sanctification, the two being inseparable. Henry presses the arrangement further. When the man was sprinkled at the start the water had blood in it; now the oil has blood under it — so that every purifying influence of the Spirit is owing to the death behind it. Wesley states the pairing plainly, the blood signifying that by which men obtain remission and the oil the graces by which they are renewed. And Ellicott reports something stronger from the later authorities: it was the putting on of the oil, above all on the head, which effected the atonement, so that if this was omitted no expiation was made however faultlessly the sacrifices had been offered.
19:
Two offerings remain, and Keil and Delitzsch note the sequencing: only when everything already described had been done could the priest turn to the sin offering, the ewe lamb being brought on account of the man's uncleanness. Gill identifies it as such by the ordinary rite of every sin offering, and takes it, as he takes all such offerings, for a figure of the one who was made sin for his people.

What sin, exactly, is a question Ellicott answers narrowly, and the answer is more humane than it first looks. The sacrifice does not expiate the state of uncleanness itself — the law elsewhere covers a man who through thoughtlessness forgot what his condition required — but the sins he committed while he was ill, and Ellicott's guess at what those were is that a man in so loathsome a state had probably given vent to impatient and unbecoming words.

Henry works from the repeated formula that the priest shall make atonement for him, and finds two things covered by it. The first is moral guilt: the sin for which the leprosy was sent is pardoned, and with it whatever he was guilty of during the affliction — and the removal of an outward trouble, Henry adds, is doubly comfortable when God gives some assurance of forgiveness alongside it, since if we have received the atonement we have reason to rejoice (Romans 5:11). The second is the ceremonial pollution that had barred him from the holy things; that is called atonement too, because restoration to the privileges of God's children is owing wholly to the great propitiation. When it is made he is clean both to his own satisfaction and in the judgment of his neighbours, retrieving his credit along with his comfort.

The burnt offering closes the rite, and closes it on a different note. Henry reads it as a thankful acknowledgment of mercy, the more due because the hand of God had been so immediately in both the sickness and the cure — which is why Christ, healing a leper, still sent him to offer what Moses commanded for a testimony (Mark 1:44). Gill worries at a smaller matter: no meat offering is named with either the trespass or the sin offering, so some held that the whole three tenth deals went up with the burnt offering, which would have been a saving to the priest if only a handful were burnt and the rest fell to his portion. Ellicott simply marks the terminus. With this the second stage ends, and the man is restored to the privileges of the sanctuary.
21:
The whole rite is now set out again at a price the poor could pay, and Keil and Delitzsch mark exactly where the concession stops. Burnt offering and sin offering come down to a pair of turtledoves or young pigeons and the flour to a single tenth of an ephah — but the trespass offering is not reduced at all, because as the consecration-offering it was the condition without which there was no reinstatement in full covenant rights. That the whole procedure is then repeated point by point rather than summarised is, on their reading, a measure of how much weight the details carried.

Ellicott sets the provision beside the other places where the law bends for poverty, and lists what is left: one lamb for the trespass offering, one tenth deal of flour, and the log of oil, which is needed for the consecration and so cannot be spared. Gill adds a further indulgence within the indulgence — if a man could not procure even the better sort of bird, the best he could get was accepted. Ellicott notes why doves were the natural substitute, being plentiful and cheap in the country.

What is not reduced matters as much as what is. Clarke states the principle without softening it: there could be no cleansing without a sacrifice, since under the law all things are purged with blood and without shedding of blood there is no remission — so even the poor man must find his lamb. Calvin comes at the same provision from the giver's side. God spares the lowly and will not have them burdened beyond their means, from which it appears that sacrifices are not valued at their intrinsic worth but by the disposition that offers in proportion to what a man has been given.

Henry draws out both edges of it. Poverty excuses no one from bringing anything at all, since God has already taken the poor into account and asks only what is in the power of the poorest to give; his commandments are not grievous, and two pigeons, when they are the utmost a man can get, are as acceptable as two lambs. But the striking thing is what did not change. Though the sacrifice was meaner, the very same ceremony was performed over it, because the souls concerned are as precious and Christ and his gospel are the same to both — and from that Henry takes the plain application, not to hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with respect of persons (James 2:1).

The earlier stage is not scaled down either. Ellicott points out that the poor man passes through the first week exactly as the rich man does, since the birds and cedar and hyssop of that stage cost little; Gill lists what that presupposes — the sprinkling with the blood and the running water, the shaving, the washing of flesh and clothes — all of it done before the eighth day comes round and the reduced offerings are brought. The closing line of the section, as Ellicott reads it, does nothing but name what has just been given: this is the law for the leper whose hand cannot reach the rest.
33:
The address changes back. Ellicott points out that the cleansing of a healed man was given to Moses alone, while this law, like those for leprous persons and garments, goes to Moses and Aaron together. It is also a law for a country the hearers had not reached. Gill and Henry both note that Israel was living in tents and had no houses, so the section stands as an appendix — Ellicott counting it the first of four laws in the book delivered prospectively, and suspecting that is why it sits after the rite of cleansing rather than beside the laws it belongs with.

Because the text says the land of Canaan, the second-Temple authorities drew a boundary around the plague and made it geographical. It was held peculiar to Palestine and unknown elsewhere; from the phrase about a house of your possession they inferred that Gentile houses were exempt, that synagogues with no dwelling attached were never visited, and that no house in Jerusalem was ever afflicted, the holy city having never been divided among the tribes. Ellicott is careful about what survives in that: whatever one makes of the reasoning, the men reporting it administered the law, and their testimony that the distemper was unknown outside Palestine and inside Jerusalem stands.

Who sends it is the sharper question, because the text says I put. Ellicott takes the plague as supernatural, proceeding from the immediate hand of God, and passes on the tradition that fixed its occasion — house-leprosy came on a man who built with materials unlawfully acquired, which the Chaldee paraphrase turns into the verse itself: if there be a man who buildeth his house with stolen goods, then I will put the plague. Clarke resists the inference. It is probably from this text that leprosy came to be thought a disease inflicted directly by God, but scripture frequently represents him as doing what in providence he only permits; his own guess is that the infection of house and garment alike proceeded from animalcula.

Calvin neither naturalises it nor softens it. He thinks we may reasonably be glad this second kind of leprosy is now unknown; a people honoured with extraordinary privileges were fittingly punished with severer penalties when they defiled the gifts in which they excelled. It was a sad thing to watch the disease invade a body, but something portentous to see it take a house and drive the owner and his family out. What God required was confession — not only when the evil had made headway but as soon as any suspicion of it existed — and behind the whole business Calvin sees a training in purity, as though God were turning away from his sanctuary anyone who came out of an unclean house.

Henry finds the warning in the address to Canaan. Even in the land of promise a house might be infected, a holy land securing nobody while so many inhabitants were unholy — as a place and a name in the visible church will not secure wicked people from God's judgments. Where sin reigns in a house it is a plague there as it is in a heart, and masters of families should fear its first appearance and take early advice.

The reporting itself is done in a fixed form, and Ellicott explains why it is so tentative. Even an owner expert enough to be certain must not tell the priest that the plague has appeared, only that something like it seems to him to have appeared, since pronouncing sentence was the priest's office and not his. Gill has him come as soon as he sees anything that gives him cause for suspicion.
36:
Nothing is examined until the house is empty. Ellicott calls the clearing a benign provision, made to save the household goods from a verdict that would otherwise have carried them with it, and argues from that alone that the law cannot have regarded the disease as infectious — a real infection would hardly have been let out of the door ahead of the inspection. Gill describes the scope of it: every person out, and every article of furniture with them. Keil and Delitzsch reason from the same detail in a different direction. Since what was in the house became unclean only once the priest had declared the house leprous, the defilement cannot have been a matter of physical contagion at all; it must have been symbolic. Wesley draws a third conclusion, and a moral one — that neither the people nor their goods were polluted before the sentence was pronounced shows what a difference God makes between sins of ignorance and sins against knowledge.

What the priest then looks for is what he looked for on skin and on cloth. Ellicott lines up the three symptoms: depressions in the wall lying lower than the surface around them, which is the same sign as in a man; and a greenish or a reddish spot, which are the second and third signs in men and garments alike. The later canons added a threshold of size, requiring the discoloured patch to be at least as large as two beans. Gill notes that the priest looks at what he is shown, the owner pointing out the place he suspects.

The verdict is deferred rather than given. Ellicott describes the seven days as a quarantine, adopted here on exactly the pattern used for an infected garment, its purpose being to see what the interval changes. Gill reads the priest's going out to the door and shutting it there as a declaration in itself: the house is not fit to be lived in while the question stands open. Keil and Delitzsch carry the procedure forward to what the seventh day may require — the stones on which the spot appears broken out and carried to an unclean place outside the town, the whole inside scraped and the dust carried after them, new stones set in and the house replastered.

Wesley stands back from the mechanics to say what he thinks the institution was. It was an extraordinary judgment peculiar to this people, and he offers three accounts of it without choosing between them: a punishment of sins more inexcusable than those of other nations, because committed against more light; or a special help to repentance granted to Israel above other peoples; or a token of the mischievous nature of sin, which the disease typifies — a thing that destroys not only persons but the very houses they live in.
39:
The second inspection is surgical. Gill describes the priest opening the house again on the seventh day and going in to see what has changed; if the marks have spread, the affected stones come out. How they came out mattered — drawn rather than knocked, Gill says, so as not to bring the building down — and never fewer than two, since on the rule he cites from Gersom a house was not shut up unless the plague showed on two stones in the first place. Then the whole inside is scraped, every wall and every stone in it, so that infection not yet visible might be taken off before it could spread; Keil and Delitzsch add the disposal, the stones and the scraped dust both carried outside the town to an unclean place, new stones set in and the house replastered.

Henry reads the operation for what it plainly is. Taking out the infected part was like cutting off a gangrened limb to preserve the rest of the body: corruption should be purged in time, before it spreads, since a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump, and if the right hand offend it is to be cut off.

Clarke lays out the whole timetable, which is easy to lose in the repetitions. Seven days shut up; if the marks have not spread, seven more; on the thirteenth day, if the infected place has grown dim or gone, the wall is opened, the piece carried out, the breach mended and the house replastered; then a third seven days; and on the nineteenth, if the plague has broken out afresh, the house comes down. Gill reports the same reckoning from Maimonides, the seventh day counting both as the last of one week and the first of the next.

Demolition is total. Keil and Delitzsch call the returning plague a malicious leprosy and have the stones, the timber and every scrap of mortar carried out of the city; Gill notes an opinion of Gersom's that the owner was to pull it down himself, with no one to help him. Henry accepts the loss as the lesser evil — a man had better be without a dwelling than live in an infected one — and takes the ruin as a picture: the leprosy of sin, if it stays obstinate under the methods of cure, will at the last be the ruin of families and churches, as Babylon unhealed was to be so forsaken that no one would take of her a stone for a corner or a stone for foundations (Jeremiah 51:26). He turns it inward as well. What remains of corruption in our mortal bodies is like this leprosy in the walls: after all our scraping and plastering we shall never be quite clear of it until the earthly house of this tabernacle is taken down (Romans 6:7). Clarke draws the same conclusion about a man who wastes the means of his own conversion — God will pull down his house, and dislodge the soul from its tabernacle.

Meanwhile the shut-up house has a law of its own, graded by how long a man stayed in it. Gill notes that nobody might enter while it stood closed, which on Jarchi's reckoning could be three weeks. Ellicott says a merely momentary entry defiled a man until sundown, and that once the priest had declared the house unclean it defiled anyone who so much as touched it from outside. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree on the next step up: to sleep there, or to eat a meal there, was graver than crossing the threshold, and cost the man the washing of his clothes as well.
48:
A house can be cured, and the test is the same one used for a man and for a garment. Ellicott states it plainly: if at the end of the second quarantine the distemper has not spread, the means prescribed having checked it, the priest declares the house clean and fit to live in again. Keil and Delitzsch say the same and put the reason in a word — the evil is healed.

What follows is the bird rite over again, and nobody pretends otherwise. Gill simply refers the reader back: the manner of cleansing a leprous house is the manner of cleansing a leprous man. Two birds, cedar wood, scarlet and hyssop; one killed into an earthen vessel over running water; the other dipped with the three accompaniments in the blood and the water; the house sprinkled seven times; the living bird released into the open field. Keil and Delitzsch note the one change of scale — the bird is let go out of the city rather than out of the camp — and Gill records a small uncertainty about who performs it, the priest himself, a fellow priest, or on some readings the master of the house.

Why a building should need atonement at all is the question Keil and Delitzsch stop over, and their answer is the theological centre of the section. The purpose here is what it was for the man: to cleanse and to make expiation. Sin shows itself first in the human body, but it does not stay there — it spreads from a man to the things he handles, uses and lives in, and the leprosy in the walls is that spread made visible. The house is therefore purified from an uncleanness that was never the house's own.

Henry arrives at the same conclusion by a different route, borrowing Bishop Patrick's phrase that the house was smitten for the man's sake, so that the owner was to reckon himself preserved by divine mercy. The houses of Israelites are spoken of as dedicated, since the nation was a holy one, and they were to be kept fit for the service of the God to whom they were devoted — from which Henry takes the domestic application, that we should reform whatever is amiss at home so that we and our houses may serve the Lord. He also passes on a reading of the whole institution as typical: the leprosy in the house standing for the idolatry that clung to the Jewish church, which the reforming kings scraped at without ever quite removing, until God took the house down and carried it into an unclean land — and that captivity proved the effectual cure.

Clarke ends the chapter on the released bird, and calls it what it evidently is. This might as well be named the scape-bird, the rites being so nearly those of the goat sent away on the day of atonement. From there he draws out the analogy that has been implicit throughout: the disease was held incurable by human means and no Jew attempted to cure it, so that what is done here does not heal the leper but declares him healed and fit for society. The guilt and power of sin can likewise be removed by no hand but God's; the body had to be sprinkled and washed and a sacrifice offered before the man could be pronounced clean; and the man pronounced clean was bound to bring his gift, as one restored to favour should offer continually the sacrifice of a grateful heart.
54:
The last four verses gather up two chapters at once. Keil and Delitzsch treat them as a single concluding formula covering both the detection of the disease and the cleansing from it; Gill runs through the list as a recapitulation — leprosy in the body, the scall of head and beard, the leprosy of a garment and of a house, and the rising and the scab and the bright spot which were the three signs in the skin.

The closing phrase about teaching draws two readings. Ellicott takes it with the sentence before, so that the whole law is given to furnish instruction against the time when the people would have to deal with these cases in the land they were entering. The ancient authorities read it more literally and got something quite different: instruction about which days the distemper may be examined on, the Chaldee paraphrase spelling it out as teaching the priests to distinguish the dark days, when a plague is not to be inspected, from the bright ones. Wesley's version of the same clause is the plainest of the three, and the most far-reaching. The rules exist to direct the priest when to pronounce clean and when unclean — so that the matter was never left to the priest's power or his will, but tied to rules so plain that the people could discern them no less than he could.

Henry closes on what the law did and did not cover. There is no repetition of it in Deuteronomy beyond a single reminder to take heed in the plague of leprosy, and the whole of it pertained to Israel alone: Naaman the Syrian, cured in Jordan, was not sent to show himself to a priest, as the Jews whom Christ healed were. Henry makes that boundary a lesson in jurisdiction — those entrusted with discipline in the church judge only those who are within, and them that are without God judgeth (1 Corinthians 5:12-13).

What remains for the reader, on his account, is a matter of self-government: to keep the mind clear of sinful affections and dispositions, which are at once its disease and its defilement, and to avoid coming within reach of the company that carries them, since God's promise to receive us is joined to a command not to touch the unclean thing (2 Corinthians 6:17). And when God who is rich in mercy has quickened us by his grace, the change is to be shown by repenting and forsaking former sins — with, Henry adds last of all, compassion for other lepers, and a desire and prayer for their cleansing too.
